title: Longest Special Path
statement:
A tree has `n` nodes labelled `0` to `n - 1` and is rooted at node `0`. Each of the `n - 1` entries `edges[i] = [u_i, v_i, length_i]` joins nodes `u_i` and `v_i` with an edge of length `length_i`, and node `i` carries the value `nums[i]`.

A *special path* runs straight down the tree from a node to one of its descendants, or is a single node on its own, and never contains two nodes with the same value. Its length is the sum of its edge lengths.

Return `[longest, fewest]`, where `longest` is the greatest length of any special path and `fewest` is the smallest number of nodes among the special paths of that length.
notes:
## Intuition

Every downward path is a stretch of a root-to-node path, so a DFS only needs the paths ending at the current node. Edges have positive lengths, so the best of those starts as high as allowed: just below the nearest node above with a repeated value. That is a variable-size sliding window over the root path: when the new node's value already sits at depth `previous`, the window's top moves to `previous + 1`. Prefix sums of the edge lengths give the window's length in O(1). A brute force that climbs from every node until a value repeats is O(n²) on a long chain.

## Approach

1. Build an undirected adjacency list `graph` of `[neighbour, length]` pairs.
2. Keep `dist[d]`, the distance from the root to the node at depth `d` of the current root path, and `lastDepth`, the depth of the deepest node on that path holding each value.
3. On entering `node`, look up `previous`, the depth of the last node above with the same value (or -1), and set `top = max(parentTop, previous + 1)`.
4. The window from depth `top` to `depth` has length `dist[depth] - dist[top]` and `depth - top + 1` nodes; it replaces `best` when it is longer, or equally long with fewer nodes.
5. Record `lastDepth[nums[node]] = depth`, visit each child with `dist[depth + 1] = dist[depth] + weight`, then restore `previous` on the way back up.
6. Return `best`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [2, 1, 2, 1, 3, 1]`. Node 0 (value 2) gives `[0, 1]`. Node 1 (value 1, distance 2) extends the window to depths 0..1, so `best = [2, 2]`. Node 2 (value 2, distance 5) repeats the root's value, so `top = 1`: length `5 - 2 = 3` with 2 nodes, `best = [3, 2]`. Node 5 (value 1, distance 11) repeats node 1 at depth 1, so `top = 2`: length `11 - 5 = 6` with 2 nodes, `best = [6, 2]`. Node 3 repeats its parent's value and is alone in its window. Node 4 (value 3, distance 6) keeps the window from the root: length 6 again but with 3 nodes, so it loses the tie. The answer is `[6, 2]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each node is entered once and does constant work besides scanning its edges.
- Space: O(n) for the graph, `dist`, `lastDepth` and the recursion.

## Pitfalls

- Restore `lastDepth` when leaving a node, or a value from a finished branch wrongly blocks its siblings.
- The top never moves back up: take the max with `parentTop`, not just `previous + 1`.
- Equal lengths go to the path with fewer nodes. A single node is a special path of length 0, so the answer is never below `[0, 1]`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `graph` | adjacency list of `[neighbour, length]` pairs |
| `dist` | `dist[d]`: root distance of the node at depth `d` on the current path |
| `lastDepth` | value → depth of its deepest node on the current path |
| `best` | `[longest length, fewest nodes]` found so far |
| `node`, `parent`, `depth` | node being visited, its parent and its depth |
| `parentTop`, `top` | window top inherited from the parent, and this node's window top |
| `previous` | depth of the last node above with the same value, or -1 |
| `length`, `count` | length and node count of the best special path ending at `node` |
| `next`, `weight` | a neighbour and the length of the edge to it |
